ASHEVILLE, North Carolina (CNN) -- In 1988, a relatively unknown rock and blues guitarist named Warren Haynes got some of his friends together to play music in Asheville, North Carolina. It was just an opportunity for local musicians to jam during the holidays, the one time of year they were all in town together. Warren Haynes' good work has been noted by the street named after him. The artists also wanted to give back to the community, so they gave the money raised by their show to various charities. The tradition has continued. Now celebrating its 20th anniversary, Haynes' Christmas Jam has evolved into an epic annual event for the musicians, fans, and particularly Habitat for Humanity. "We need Habitat For Humanity more now than ever, with the whole mortgage crisis that put us where we are now, and the fact that Habitat is about building homes for people that can't afford homes as opposed to lending money to people who can't afford homes," Haynes told CNN. Haynes and his wife, Stefani Scamardo, decided to donate 100 percent of the Christmas Jam proceeds to Habitat for Humanity years ago because they could see exactly where the money was going. They go back each year and meet the families they helped build homes for. Singer Joan Osborne echoed Haynes' thoughts. "It's a scary time. A lot of people are losing their homes so it's good to be able to do something that helps with that specific problem," she said. Going into 2008's shows, which were held December 12 and 13, the Christmas Jam had raised more than $665,000 for Asheville's Habitat For Humanity. The money has gone into building 12 houses in Enka Hills, a wooded community surrounded by mountains on a street the organization appropriately named Warren Haynes Drive. (In 2005 Habitat also built a house in the New Orleans Musicians Village.) The Thursday before the show, Haynes presented the key to a new home to single mother Suzie Cromer and her 8-year-old daughter. "Meeting the families and seeing the work that Habitat's doing with our help -- you know its hard to see that and not get emotional," Haynes said. "Warren is a hero in our mind," said Habitat's Arianne Kjellquist. "In western North Carolina, the housing costs are really out of whack with what the local wages are, so there's a big discrepancy there. There are more people that maybe would have been approved previously when the lending standards weren't so strict." This year's Christmas Jam lived up to the long-lasting and crowd-pleasing traditions of previous shows. The first night's show ran more than nine hours, ending with an Allman Brothers set after 4 a.m. The second night's show ended at 3:30 a.m. Performers included Ben Harper and Relentless 7, Travis Tritt, Michael Franti, Osborne, Ivan Neville's Dumpstaphunk, Steve Earle and Haynes' band Gov't Mule. Perhaps the most anticipated addition this year among both fans and artists was former Led Zeppelin member John Paul Jones, who played acoustic mandolin, bass and keyboards throughout the weekend with just about everyone. Jones said he was happy to pitch in. "In the economic climate like this, people really just want to get out and enjoy themselves and forget about the day to day stuff that they have to deal with. So it works on many levels," Jones said. "The fact that it is for a good cause is just a huge bonus." Haynes says the 20-year evolution of the Christmas Jam reflects his career. "We've grown up together. Its a parallel of the progress that I have achieved, and the event reflects not only the philosophy I share with these people but the mission." And as fans danced the night away while the artists played their hearts out, families' dreams of owning their perfect home come true. "I would have never imagined or dreamed that it would turn into what its turned into," Haynes reflected with a huge smile.

Outdoor enthusiasts flock to Asheville, North Carolina, to hike the Appalachian Trail, chase hidden waterfalls, and paddle along the ancient waters of the French Broad River.

Yet, Asheville’s magnetic pull extends far beyond its natural beauty. The city boasts a rich history and a distinctly creative soul. At the heart of its historical legacy is the Biltmore Estate, built by George Washington Vanderbilt II in the late 19th century. In downtown Asheville, history takes on a different form. The River Arts District, a former industrial zone along the river, now houses hundreds of working artists, sculptors, and potters who open their studios to the public, exemplifying the city's vibrant, bohemian spirit.

Asheville has also earned a worldwide reputation as a culinary and craft beer epicenter. Proudly holding the title of "Beer City, USA," it boasts more breweries per capita than almost any other city in the country. **Music with a mission: Warren Haynes’ 20th Christmas Jam brings hope amid housing crisis**

**By Chris Vance, CNN**
**ASHEVILLE, North Carolina (CNN) —** As the nation grapples with a staggering financial crisis, widespread foreclosures, and an increasingly grim economic outlook, a quiet mountain town in North Carolina became the center of a very loud, very soulful response this weekend. 

For two decades, guitar virtuoso Warren Haynes has gathered a revolving cast of rock, blues, and country royalty in his hometown of Asheville for the annual Christmas Jam. But as the event celebrated its landmark 20th anniversary on Saturday night, the music carried a weight far heavier than just holiday cheer.

With the 2008 subprime mortgage collapse leaving millions of Americans at risk of losing their shelter, this year's concert—which benefits Asheville Area Habitat for Humanity—felt less like a simple charity show and more like an urgent lifeline.

"Given everything that's happening with the economy right now, people need help more than ever," Haynes told CNN backstage at the packed Asheville Civic Center. "When we started this 20 years ago in a small club, we just wanted to play music with our friends and give back a little bit. We never imagined we’d be standing here two decades later, building entire neighborhoods during a national housing crisis."

### A marathon of music for a nation in need

What began in 1988 as a modest gathering of local musicians has evolved into one of the most respected benefit concerts in the United States. The 20th-anniversary lineup reflected that stature, featuring a marathon, seven-hour showcase of talent. 

Haynes’ own band, Gov't Mule, anchored a night that included electrifying performances by blues legend Johnny Winter, slide-guitar prodigy Derek Trucks, Susan Tedeschi, roots-rockers Coheed and Cambria, and Michael Franti. True to the festival’s reputation, the night was defined by spontaneous, once-in-a-lifetime collaborations, with artists stepping on and off stage to jam well into the early morning hours.

Yet, despite the arena-sized riffs and party atmosphere, the stark reality of 2008 was never far from the crowd's mind. Between sets, video screens displayed images not of rock stars, but of local families holding the keys to their very first homes—homes built by the proceeds of past Jams.

### Building homes while the market crumbles

The timing of this year's milestone could not be more critical. The U.S. housing market is enduring its worst downturn since the Great Depression, with national foreclosure rates spiking by more than 70 percent over the past year. As traditional bank loans dry up and low-income families are squeezed out of the market, non-profit organizations like Habitat for Humanity are facing unprecedented demand.

To date, the Christmas Jam has raised over $1.3 million for the local Habitat chapter, making it the organization's largest single annual fundraiser. Those funds have directly financed the construction of more than 25 homes in the Asheville area, including an entire subdivision known as "Structure Lane," where street names bear subtle nods to the concert's musical heritage.

"In a year where the word 'housing' has become synonymous with crisis, panic, and foreclosures, the Christmas Jam represents the exact opposite," said Lew Holloway, Executive Director of Asheville Area Habitat for Humanity. "Warren and his wife, Stefani Scamardo, have created a sustainable model of community giving. The money raised here tonight doesn't just put a roof over someone's head; it stabilizes families at a time when the ground beneath them is shaking."

Unlike traditional charitable endeavors that rely on wealthy corporate donors—many of whom have scaled back giving during the current recession—the Christmas Jam relies on music fans. Tickets for the 20th-anniversary event sold out in minutes, drawing fans from all 50 states and several foreign countries. 

Furthermore, the musicians themselves perform for free, and many stay in town for an extra day to put on hard hats, pick up hammers, and work directly on the Habitat build sites alongside the future homeowners.

### A blueprint for hope

For the families on the receiving end, the impact of the Jam is life-changing. 

"With everything falling apart in the news, you start to feel like nobody is looking out for the working person," said Maria Gonzalez, a local healthcare worker who is scheduled to move into a Christmas Jam-funded home early next year. "To know that musicians and fans came together to give my children a safe place to sleep—it’s a miracle. It gives you faith."

As the final notes of an all-star encore echoed through the Civic Center early Sunday morning, Haynes reflected on the legacy of the past 20 years and the uncertain road ahead for the country. 

"Music has always had the power to heal, but it also has the power to build," Haynes said, wiping sweat from his forehead. "Things are tough out there right now. But as long as we have a stage, a few guitars, and people who care, we’re going to keep building."

For an economy in desperate need of a turnaround, the 20th Christmas Jam provided more than just a night of world-class rock and roll—it offered a resounding reminder of what can be accomplished when a community tunes into the same chord.

# Special Report: From Local Holiday Reunion to Musical Institution—The Evolution of Warren Haynes’ Christmas Jam

**Prepared by:** Arts & Music Industry Analysis  
**Topic:** The History, Philanthropy, and Musical Legacy of Warren Haynes’ Christmas Jam  
**Location Focus:** Asheville, North Carolina  

---

## Executive Summary

What began in 1988 as an informal, end-of-year gathering of Asheville-area musicians has transformed over three and a half decades into one of the most celebrated and enduring charity benefit concerts in American music history. Spearheaded by Grammy Award-winning guitarist and singer-songwriter Warren Haynes (Gov’t Mule, The Allman Brothers Band), the **Christmas Jam** has evolved into a multi-day cultural event. 

To date, the festival has raised over **$2.8 million** for the Asheville Area Habitat for Humanity, helping construct dozens of homes and fund entire infrastructure projects for local families in need. Renowned for its marathon setlists, unexpected supergroup collaborations, and late-night improvisational sets, the Christmas Jam stands as a masterclass in how community roots can fuel national philanthropic impact.

---

## 1. Origins: The 1988 "Snow Jam"

In December 1988, Warren Haynes—then a rising guitarist playing with Dickey Betts before joining the re-formed Allman Brothers Band in 1989—returned to his hometown of Asheville, North Carolina, for the holidays. Wanting to catch up and play music with local friends who were also home from the road, Haynes organized an unadvertised, loose jam session at a local venue called **45 Cherry**.

Originally dubbed the "Snow Jam," the event was simple:
* **The Concept:** A "reunion show" for local and regional musicians.
* **The Admission:** A small cover charge or pass-the-hat collection.
* **The Beneficiary:** Local charities, primarily food banks and toy drives in its first few years.

There was no grand marketing strategy; the night was propelled entirely by word-of-mouth and the camaraderie of the Blue Ridge musical community. However, as Haynes’ own national profile expanded throughout the 1990s with the Allman Brothers Band and the formation of Gov’t Mule, the guest list began to grow exponentially.

---

## 2. The Philanthropic Engine: Partnering with Habitat for Humanity

By the late 1990s, the event had outgrown intimate club venues like *Be Here Now* and moved to the historic **Thomas Wolfe Auditorium**, before eventually taking over the 7,600-capacity **ExploreAsheville.com Arena** (formerly the U.S. Cellular Center).

As the scale expanded, Haynes sought a primary charitable partner that could deliver long-term, tangible results for the local Asheville community. In 1999, the Christmas Jam officially aligned with the **Asheville Area Habitat for Humanity**.

```
CHRISTMAS JAM FINANCIAL & COMMUNITY IMPACT AT A GLANCE
------------------------------------------------------
• Total Funds Raised:       Over $2,800,000+
• Homes Constructed:        50+ single-family homes fully funded
• Additional Infrastructure: Funded "Jam Town" subdivisions & green building initiatives
• Volunteer Hours:         Thousands of artist and fan hours logged on build sites
```

The partnership created a unique ecosystem where concert proceeds directly fund the **"Housing to Homeownership"** program. Haynes and participating artists do not merely write checks; they regularly visit active construction sites during the event weekend, wielding hammers alongside future homeowners.

---

## 3. The Marathon Experience: Anatomy of a Christmas Jam

Musically, the Christmas Jam is legendary for its endurance format and genre-defying lineups. Unlike standard multi-act festivals with rigid time limits, Haynes encourages an open-ended, collaborative atmosphere.

### Key Musical Characteristics:
* **Marathon Length:** Shows typically begin in the early evening (around 6:00 PM) and frequently push past **3:00 AM or 4:00 AM**, spanning 8 to 10 hours of continuous live music.
* **The "Pre-Jam":** Held the night before the main event (often at the intimate Orange Peel club), serving as a warm-up where artists test out unscripted jams and unique pairings.
* **Spontaneous Collaborations:** Unrehearsed sit-ins are the baseline, not the exception. The backstage area serves as a living room where blues, rock, bluegrass, and soul icons cross paths.

Over the decades, the stage has hosted a historic roster including Dave Grohl, Gregg Allman, Bob Weir, Trey Anastasio, Peter Frampton, Grace Potter, Marcus King, Eric Church, Sheryl Crow, and Billy Gibbons.

---

## 4. Voice of the Stage: Artist Testimonials

**HARMONY IN THE HARD TIMES: HOW WARREN HAYNES’ CHRISTMAS JAM RAISED $665,000 FOR HABITAT AMIDST ECONOMIC CRISIS**

**By Music & Charity Feature Desk**
**Late December 2008**

**ASHEVILLE, N.C.** — As a turbulent 2008 draws to a close, the headlines dominating the evening news are stark: Wall Street bailouts, skyrocketing unemployment, and a subprime mortgage crisis that has left millions of American families facing foreclosure. Yet in the Blue Ridge Mountains of Western North Carolina, a very different story unfolded this month—one where guitars, soul, and solidarity provided a vital buffer against the prevailing economic storm.

Marking its milestone 20th anniversary, Warren Haynes’ annual Christmas Jam has evolved from a humble gathering of local musicians into one of the most respected, star-studded benefit concerts in the nation. But this year’s milestone was defined by more than just legendary marathon jam sessions; it was defined by a record-breaking check. 

At a time when non-profits across the country are seeing donations dry up, the Christmas Jam presented a staggering **$665,000** to the Asheville Area Habitat for Humanity—the largest single donation in the event’s history, bringing its cumulative total to over $2.8 million.

For Haynes—the guitar virtuoso and tireless frontman for Gov’t Mule and mainstay of The Allman Brothers Band—the achievement is both humbling and urgently necessary. 

"When we started this thing 20 years ago, it was just an excuse for a bunch of local friends to get together and play music around the holidays," Haynes reflected backstage at the Asheville Civic Center. "We never imagined it would grow into an institution that could literally build entire neighborhoods for families who need them."

### From Local Gig to National Institution

The Christmas Jam’s origins date back to 1988, when it was dubbed the "Christmas Sunshine Jam," hosted in cozy local venues like the 828 Club. Over two decades, through word of mouth and Haynes’ legendary rolodex, the Jam transformed. It moved from small clubs to the historic Orange Peel, and ultimately to the sold-out, 7,000-seat Asheville Civic Center. 

What makes the Jam unique in the festival landscape is the spirit of volunteerism. The artists—which over the years have ranged from Dave Matthews and Gregg Allman to Peter Frampton and Trey Anastasio—donate their time and talent. Stagehands, security, and production crews work pro bono. Because expenses are kept to a minimum, nearly every dollar from ticket sales, auctions, and merchandise goes directly into buying land, lumber, and drywall.

This year’s two-night 20th-anniversary bash on December 12 and 13 was a triumph of American roots music. Fans were treated to unforgettable collaborations featuring Gov't Mule, The Derek Trucks Band, Susan Tedeschi, Steve Miller, Johnny Winter, Michael Franti, and Coheed and Cambria. But while the music stretched late into the night, the true heart of the event remained focused on the daytime reality facing the local community.

### Housing Crisis Makes Mission Urgent

The $665,000 windfall could not have come at a more crucial moment. The national recession has hit working-class families in Western North Carolina with devastating force. As traditional home loans evaporate and wages stall, the dream of safe, affordable housing has shifted from a difficult goal to an outright emergency.

"The housing crisis isn't just a abstract concept on Wall Street; it’s happening right here on Main Street," said a representative from Asheville Area Habitat for Humanity during the check presentation. "Because of the national economic slump, the need for safe, affordable shelter in our region has skyrocketed. What Warren, his wife Stefani Scamardo, and this music community are doing isn't just giving money—they are quite literally keeping roofs over children's heads when they need it most."

The funds raised from the Christmas Jam are earmarked to continue development on entire Habitat subdivisions in the region, such as the Enka Hills community. These homes aren’t handouts; Habitat partner families invest hundreds of hours of "sweat equity" building their own homes and those of their neighbors, purchasing them with zero-interest mortgages. 

In a year where the phrase "mortgage" has become synonymous with anxiety, the Christmas Jam model offers a ray of hope: sustainable, community-backed homeownership that cannot be undermined by predatory lending.

### Rebuilding, One Note at a Time

For the thousands of fans who packed into the Civic Center—and the hundreds of thousands more who listened via radio broadcasts—the 2008 Christmas Jam was a powerful reminder of what music can achieve when divorced from corporate greed. In a year defined by loss, Asheville proved that community spirit remains solvent.

As the final chords of the traditional all-star finale of "I Shall Be Released" echoed through the arena in the early morning hours, the message was clear. The economy may be in a recession, but empathy, music, and the drive to help one's neighbor are in a booming bull market.

"Music has always been a healing force," Haynes said before stepping offstage into the chilly mountain air. "To know that the music we played tonight is going to turn into hammer and nails, into front doors and bedrooms for kids who need them... there’s no better Christmas gift than that."
